info.name: InsuredMine Node.js Assessment
info.description:
Click-through test guide for every feature. Run requests TOP TO BOTTOM, inside each folder, in order — later requests reuse ids saved automatically by earlier ones (jobId, userId, scheduledMessageId), so skipping ahead will fail with a 404/empty result, not because the API is broken.

Before you start:
1. Make sure the server is running (see README 'Running the app').
2. Set the `baseUrl` variable below if your server isn't on localhost:3000.
3. Run '0. Health Check' first to confirm the server is reachable at all.

item.name: 0. Health Check
item.description: Confirms the server is up before you test anything else. If this fails, the app isn't running — go run `npm start` first.

item.name: GET Server is alive?

request.description:
Expected: 200 OK, { success: true, data: { status: 'up', pid, uptimeSec } }.
If this fails to connect at all, the server isn't running - start it with `npm start`.

item.name: 1. Upload the spreadsheet (Task 1.1)
item.description: Feature: you give it the CSV file of insurance records. It reads the file and saves it into MongoDB, split across 6 organized tables (Agents, Users, Accounts, Categories, Carriers, Policies). This runs on a background worker thread so the server doesn't freeze while it works - that's why the upload request returns instantly with a jobId, and you poll a separate request to see when it's actually done.

item.name: 1a. POST Upload the CSV file

formdata.description: Click 'Select Files' and choose: docs/data-sheet - Node js Assesment (2) (1).csv from the project folder

request.description:
IMPORTANT: click into the 'file' row's value cell and select the CSV file from the project's docs/ folder before sending.

Expected: 202 Accepted, with a jobId. This is saved automatically into the {{jobId}} variable for the next request - the upload itself keeps running in the background after this responds.

item.name: 1b. GET Check upload progress/result

request.description:
Run this AFTER 1a. Uses the jobId that 1a saved automatically.

Run it a few times, a couple seconds apart, until status changes from 'processing' to 'completed'.

Expected on success: status: 'completed', errors: [], and insertedCounts showing real numbers, e.g. policies: 1198 for the full sheet.

exec: if (status === 'completed') { pm.test('Upload completed with no errors', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().data.errors).to.have.lengthOf(0)); }

item.name: 1c. (Repeat) Upload the SAME file again - proves no duplicates

request.description:
Optional but a good test: re-upload the exact same file. Then re-run 1b with the NEW jobId this returns.

Expected: the insertedCounts (e.g. policies: 1198) stay exactly the same as before - proving the app doesn't create duplicate records when a file is uploaded twice.

item.name: 1d. (Negative test) Upload with no file -> should fail cleanly

request.description:
Sends the request with NO file attached, on purpose.

Expected: 400 Bad Request with a clear error message - NOT a 500 crash. This proves the API validates input properly instead of blowing up.

exec: pm.test('Rejected with 400, not a crash', () => pm.response.to.have.status(400));

item.name: 2. Search a person's policies (Task 1.2)
item.description: Feature: look up all insurance policies belonging to someone by typing part of their name (there's no 'username' field in the data, so this searches the person's name instead).

item.name: 2a. GET Search by name (e.g. 'lura')

query.description: Try any first name from the CSV file - partial match, case-insensitive

request.description:
Run this AFTER Step 1 (you need data uploaded first, or this will return an empty list).

Expected: 200 OK with a list of policies for that person, each showing carrier, category, and agent details filled in (not just raw ids).

item.name: 2b. (Negative test) Search with NO name -> should fail cleanly

request.description:
No 'username' query param, on purpose.

Expected: 400 Bad Request saying username is required. This is CORRECT behavior, not a bug - the API is supposed to reject this.

item.name: 3. Totals per user (Task 1.3)
item.description: Feature: for every person, shows how many policies they have and their total premium (price) added up - computed live from the database, not stored separately.

item.name: 3a. GET Aggregated totals for all users

request.description:
Run this AFTER Step 1.

Expected: 200 OK with a list of users, each showing totalPolicies and totalPremium. This also saves the first userId found into {{userId}} for the next request.

exec: console.log('userId saved for next request:', pm.collectionVariables.get('userId'));

item.name: 3b. GET Aggregated totals for ONE user

request.description:
Run this AFTER 3a (uses the userId it saved).

Expected: 200 OK with that one user's totalPolicies, totalPremium, and full policy list with category/carrier names filled in.

item.name: 3c. (Negative test) Aggregate with a fake/invalid userId

request.description:
Sends a made-up, invalid id on purpose.

Expected: 400 Bad Request saying 'Invalid userId' - not a crash.

item.name: 4. CPU monitor auto-restart (Task 2.1)
item.description: Feature: watches how hard the server's CPU is working. If it stays very busy (70%+) for a sustained stretch, the app shuts itself down cleanly and automatically starts a fresh copy - like an auto-restart safety net. You can't fully SEE this in Postman alone (it happens in the server's terminal logs) - this request just triggers it. See the instructions below for what to watch for.

item.name: 4a. GET Trigger CPU stress (dev-only demo endpoint)

request.description:
This deliberately makes the CPU work hard for 20 seconds, purely to demo the restart feature - it is NOT a normal production API (it's disabled entirely when NODE_ENV=production).

HOW TO WATCH THE FEATURE WORK:
1. Send this request.
2. Immediately switch to the terminal window where `npm start` is running.
3. Within a few seconds you'll see log lines like:
   'CPU usage above threshold ... consecutive: 1'
   'CPU usage above threshold ... consecutive: 2'
   'CPU usage above threshold ... consecutive: 3'
   'CPU threshold sustained -> triggering restart'
   'Starting graceful shutdown' -> 'Worker exited' -> 'Forking replacement worker...' -> 'Server listening on port 3000'
4. That whole sequence is the feature working: hot CPU -> clean shutdown -> automatic restart.

This request itself will just return a 200 once the 20s finishes - the interesting part is the SERVER LOGS, not this response.

exec: pm.test('200 OK after the stress finishes', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: 4b. GET Confirm the server restarted (different pid)

request.description:
Run this AFTER 4a has finished and you've seen the restart in the logs.

Expected: still 200 OK and status 'up', but with a DIFFERENT pid than before 4a - proof it's a freshly restarted process, not the same one that was running earlier. Compare it against the pid from '0. Health Check' at the very start.

item.name: 5. Schedule a message for later (Task 2.2)
item.description: Feature: you tell it 'save this message into the database at this exact date/time in the future', and it actually does it right on schedule - even if the server restarts in between (that's Task 2.1 above). This proves the schedule is stored safely in the database, not just held in memory.

item.name: 5a. POST Schedule a message ~2 minutes from now

request.description:
A 'Pre-request Script' on this request automatically fills in {{scheduleDay}} and {{scheduleTime}} with a real date/time about 2 minutes from right now (in UTC) - you don't need to type a date by hand.

Expected: 201 Created, status: 'pending'. The returned _id is saved automatically for the next request.

item.name: 5b. GET Check the scheduled message (run right after 5a)

request.description: Run this right after 5a. Expected: status: 'pending' (it hasn't reached its scheduled time yet).

item.name: 5c. GET Check again AFTER waiting ~2+ minutes -> should be delivered

request.description:
WAIT about 2-3 minutes after running 5a, THEN send this.

Expected: status changes to 'completed', and resultingMessageId is now filled in - it delivered itself automatically, with no further action from you.

exec: console.log('Status:', data.status, '- if still pending, wait longer and resend this request.');

item.name: 5d. GET List all scheduled messages (filter by status)

request.description: Lists messages by status. Change 'pending' to 'completed' in the URL to see delivered ones.

item.name: 5e. (Negative test) Schedule with a time already in the past

request.description:
Uses a date from the past, on purpose.

Expected: 400 Bad Request saying the resolved schedule time is in the past - correct behavior, not a bug.

item.name: 6. BONUS - Prove a restart doesn't lose a scheduled message

request.description:
This is the most impressive combined test - it proves Task 2.1 and Task 2.2 work correctly TOGETHER.

STEPS:
1. Send this request (schedules a message ~2 min out, same as 5a).
2. Immediately go run '4a. GET Trigger CPU stress' from folder 4 to force a restart.
3. Wait past the scheduled time (check the server logs to confirm it restarted).
4. Use '5c'-style check (GET /messages/schedule/{{scheduledMessageId}}) to confirm status is still 'completed' despite the restart in between.

This proves scheduled messages are saved safely in the database, not lost when the server restarts.

exec: console.log('Now go run 4a to trigger the restart, then wait and re-check this id:', body.data._id);
